summary: Tiagabine is an antiepileptic drug used as adjunctive therapy in the treatment of partial (focal) seizures in adults and children 12 years and older. It works by selectively blocking the GAT-1 transporter that normally takes GABA back up into neurons and glia, thereby increasing inhibitory GABAergic activity. It must be titrated slowly from a low starting dose and is taken with food to blunt rapid absorption. An important safety issue is that tiagabine has caused new-onset seizures and status epilepticus in patients WITHOUT epilepsy who were given it off-label (for example, for psychiatric or pain conditions); it should generally be reserved for its approved epilepsy indication and used cautiously off-label. Other key effects include dizziness, somnolence, asthenia, tremor, difficulty concentrating, and a class risk of suicidal thoughts and behavior. Hepatic metabolism (CYP3A4) means enzyme-inducing antiepileptics lower its levels.
indications: Adjunctive therapy in the treatment of partial (focal) seizures in adults and children 12 years of age and older

moa: Tiagabine is a selective inhibitor of GABA reuptake. By binding to and blocking the GAT-1 sodium-dependent GABA transporter on presynaptic neurons and surrounding glial cells, it prevents the normal reuptake of released gamma-aminobutyric acid (GABA), the principal inhibitory neurotransmitter in the CNS. This increases the concentration and prolongs the action of GABA in the synaptic cleft, enhancing GABA-mediated inhibitory neurotransmission and raising the threshold for seizure activity. It does not act directly as a GABA-receptor agonist; its effect depends on endogenous GABA release.

preg: There are no adequate, well-controlled studies in pregnant women, and animal studies showed developmental toxicity. Use during pregnancy only if the potential benefit justifies the risk. Do not abruptly discontinue antiepileptic therapy, as seizures may harm both mother and fetus. Enroll in a pregnancy registry where available.
lact: It is not known whether tiagabine is excreted in human milk; it is excreted in the milk of lactating rats. Because of the potential for serious adverse reactions in the nursing infant, use with caution and weigh the benefit of breastfeeding against the benefit of therapy.
renal: No specific dosage adjustment is required for renal impairment; tiagabine pharmacokinetics are not substantially altered in renal dysfunction.
hepatic: Clearance of tiagabine is reduced in patients with liver disease, leading to higher and more prolonged plasma concentrations. Reduce the dose and/or lengthen the dosing interval in patients with hepatic impairment, and monitor closely for CNS effects.

major: Enzyme-inducing antiepileptic drugs (carbamazepine, phenytoin, phenobarbital, primidone) - induce CYP3A4 and roughly double tiagabine clearance, lowering its levels; non-induced patients need much lower doses
moderate: Strong CYP3A4 inhibitors - may increase tiagabine exposure
Valproate - modestly increases free tiagabine and tiagabine slightly lowers valproate levels
Other antiepileptics / drugs lowering seizure threshold
minor: No significant effect on the pharmacokinetics of oral contraceptives, warfarin, digoxin, theophylline, or cimetidine
interactions.food: Take with food; food slows the rate of absorption (lower peak) without reducing total exposure, improving tolerability.
interactions.alcohol: Avoid alcohol - additive CNS depression and impaired alertness.
interactions.diagnostics: May cause EEG abnormalities; can be associated with nonconvulsive status (spike-and-wave stupor).

counsel: Take this medicine with food, exactly as prescribed, and do not change the dose or stop suddenly on your own
It can make you dizzy, sleepy, or less able to concentrate - do not drive or operate machinery until you know how it affects you, and avoid alcohol
Tell your doctor right away about any new or worsening seizures, episodes of confusion or staring, or feeling very weak
Report any new or worsening depression, anxiety, agitation, or thoughts of harming yourself
This medicine is meant for epilepsy; if you were given it for another condition, be alert for new seizures and tell your prescriber
Carry information that you take an anti-seizure medicine and keep regular follow-up appointments

pearls: Has caused NEW-ONSET seizures and status epilepticus in patients WITHOUT epilepsy given it off-label - reserve for approved adjunctive epilepsy use and watch for seizures if used otherwise
Take WITH food to blunt the rapid peak and reduce dizziness
Enzyme-inducing AEDs roughly double clearance - patients NOT on inducers need much lower doses and slower titration
Can cause nonconvulsive status epilepticus (spike-wave stupor) - consider EEG for unexplained confusion
Class suicidality warning for antiepileptics - monitor mood
Taper rather than stop abruptly to avoid withdrawal/rebound seizures
missed: If you miss a dose, take it as soon as you remember unless it is almost time for the next dose, in which case skip the missed dose - do not take two doses at once. Do not stop taking tiagabine without talking to your doctor, as stopping suddenly can cause seizures.
overdose: Reported overdose symptoms include somnolence, impaired consciousness, agitation, confusion, speech difficulty, hostility, depression, weakness, myoclonus, seizures, status epilepticus, and respiratory depression. There is no specific antidote; treatment is supportive, including airway protection, and seizures/status managed with standard measures. Because tiagabine is highly protein bound, dialysis is unlikely to be beneficial. Consider activated charcoal for recent ingestion.
